As Williams grew to a higher volume of projects, their back-office processes couldn’t keep pace. Job cost data between their Vista ERP and Procore project management software didn’t sync in a way that worked for the business, forcing the accounting team to rely on manual workarounds.

日本の担い手.quote: Metoki: Today's theme is Agave Syrup x Tequila. "Agave syrup" has really started appearing everywhere lately. We've invited Ms. Yabuta, who was the first to import such agave syrup into Japan!

Yabuta: It has been 19 years since I first imported agave syrup to Japan in 2006. At the time, I would have been thrilled if there was even one type of agave syrup in a supermarket, but now I'm happy to see supermarkets that carry several types. In supermarkets, it is sometimes sold alongside the organic section, the sugar section, or with honey.
Yabuta: You might be surprised, but it goes well with Japanese food!

Metoki: Mole means sauce in Spanish, and this is a meat dish covered in a sauce containing cacao. Cacao is also native to Mexico. Since cacao itself isn't sweet, it's often used in cooking. This dish also has a sweet sauce, so many people in Japan might be surprised at first.

Tepito Chef Kumi: What Japanese people imagine when they hear "taco" might be the Western-style hard type of tortilla. The Mexican style is the soft type made from corn. It's also easier to wrap the ingredients.

Metoki: Speaking of Mexican-style ingredients, I think I like cactus! You've started to see cactus salad here and there in Japan, too. As we mentioned earlier regarding veganism, 'vegetarian tacos' for vegetarians are also becoming popular. Those tacos sometimes even contain cactus as an ingredient.

Yabuta: Speaking of Mexico, there's also avocado! Delicious avocados are becoming easier to get in Japan, so you can enjoy making guacamole at home. It's easy to make just by mashing the avocado and mixing it with salt and lime, so I often make it at home too.
Metoki: I make guacamole often, too. Although, once you know the price of avocados in Mexico, you can't help but think the avocados you buy in Japan are expensive (laughs).
Gracias mangoes can be bought cheaply in Mexico, but they are quite expensive in Japan. I'm really happy to be able to get a taste of Mexico today!

Metoki: I often buy pork cheek, and there are quite a lot of Mexican-produced ones lined up at the supermarket. I combine that pork cheek with Mexican asparagus or avocado, and sometimes I make a meal using only Mexican ingredients to enjoy a Mexican vibe even in Japan.

Also, there's the hot sauce that Mexican people put on various dishes. You don't see it much in Japan, but in Mexico, it's normally placed on the tables at restaurants. When you add it, it instantly feels like Mexico~! (laughs).

Yabuta: You can get Mexican ingredients in Japan, and the opportunities to experience the vibe are increasing. Agave syrup is also becoming more accessible, so if you're interested, I hope you'll try using it. We'd be happy if you could use our usage methods as a reference.
